surfaces.part: terrain tile fill (dark teal water/grass autotile, full 16x16 block)

answer.evidence: The candidate is a full 16x16 opaque terrain tile. The left columns show a grey and green edge strip and the rest is dark teal water with slight pixel variation and a few lighter highlight pixels. The column scan shows one uniform run over rows 0-15 at every sampled column, so there is no front-edge line, eave shadow, ellipse or vertical front face. It is a flat ground/water autotile and not a standing object, so it has no top-plus-front structure.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are fine: 9 visible tones per tile against 3 for the reference grass, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the edges are tinted rather than black. But the picture does not back this up. The candidate renders as a small, dark teal block with a lighter strip along its left edge, far smaller than a 4x3 tile patch. It has no visible grass tufts or clumps, and no per-blade or soil grain like the reference grass. The interior reads as large flat areas of one dark teal, and the 20% near-flat coverage against 0% for both references confirms this. The shading shows about 4 steps against the references' 5-6. By eye it carries less information than the grass reference, and it looks more like a plain fill than a lakeside grass mask. When in doubt, fail.

answer.evidence: This is a 16x16 autotile terrain tile. The left columns are green grass, followed by a lighter teal shore edge. The rest is uniform dark teal water with slight noise and one light pixel near row 12. All three column scans run unbroken through rows 0-15 with the same lightness, so there are no bands, edge lines, eave shadows, ellipses or front face. It is a flat ground/water fill, not a standing object, so it reads as a top-down slab by the measurement rules.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate renders very small on the board: a dark teal water or grass patch with a lighter edge strip and a thin highlight. By eye it is mostly one dark body tone, and I read about 4-5 lightness steps, so it is not as richly clumped as the Beodeul grass. The measured facts still favour it. It has 9 visible tones per tile against 3 for the grass reference and 7 for the paving. Near-flat coverage is 20%, which is low enough that it does not count as flat fills. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline leans teal/green like the material rather than being a black sticker line. The limits are only 9 colours in total and little grain in the body. On the primary facts it is at or above the references with tinted outlines, so I pass it, narrowly.

surfaces.part: lake/water terrain tile (flat fill with a lighter left edge strip, x~4-6 and a few speckle pixels)

answer.evidence: The image is a full 16x16 opaque terrain tile: a grass strip on the left (x~4-6), then a dark teal water fill with sparse lighter speckles. The column scan shows one uniform run of rows 0-15 at x=4, 8 and 11, with no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no ellipse. It is a flat ground/water autotile with no standing volume and no vertical front face, so it reads as a flat top-down surface, which is normal for terrain.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a very small, dark teal block with a pale strip on its left edge. It should be a 4x3 lake-edge grass patch, but it reads as a mostly uniform fill with little grass clumping or grain. The measured facts look fine on paper: 9 visible tones per tile against 3 for the grass reference, 0% neutral dark edges, and 20% near-flat coverage. But the whole piece has only 9 distinct colours in total, so it has roughly 4 usable shading steps against the reference's 5-6. By eye its large areas are flat compared with the grass reference's dotted tufts, which have 0% flat coverage. There is no clear dark-material outline, and form is carried by the edge strip alone. At this scale it would look flatter next to the reference, and when in doubt it fails.
